questions.q: What are the three primary activities involved in caring about and studying plants (alongside understanding ecosystems and plant functions)?
options: Cataloging (naming, describing, recording, monitoring), Identifying (recognizing, keying), and Classifying (grouping, ranking)
Clearcutting, Stumpage Valuation, and Monopsony Pricing
Digitizing, Rasterizing, and Georeferencing
Hybridizing, Cloning, and Genetic Modification

questions.q: How has 'Plant Taxonomy' evolved from classic taxonomy to modern systematics, and why might plant names differ among different floras?
options: Classic taxonomy grouped plants based on similar anatomy (floral characteristics, fruits, etc.), whereas modern taxonomy is revised as we learn more about plant evolution and genetics, causing names to differ across floras
Classic taxonomy used DNA sequencing, whereas modern taxonomy groups plants strictly by their Raunkiaer growth form
Plant names never change once published by European explorers in the 18th century
Floras use different names because each province is required to invent its own Latin genus names

questions.q: In botanical nomenclature, what suffix do standard modern plant Family names end with, and what are the older alternative family names for Asteraceae and Apiaceae?
options: Modern family names end in '-aceae'; older floras use alternative family names ending in '-ae', such as Compositae (for Asteraceae) and Umbelliferae (for Apiaceae)
Modern family names end in '-ae'; older floras use '-aceae' such as Ericaceae and Salicaceae
Modern family names end in '-ii' or '-yi'; older family names end in '-um'
Family names have no standardized suffix in the International Code of Botanical Nomenclature

questions.q: How did scientific species names transition under Linnaeus, and what grammatical rule often applies to the specific epithet (e.g., Lilium philadelphicum)?
options: They transitioned from long descriptive polynomial names to binomial names (Genus + specific epithet), where the suffix of the descriptive specific epithet often agrees with the genus name
They transitioned from two-word binomial names to 20-word polynomial paragraphs
The specific epithet is always capitalized and precedes the family name
The specific epithet must always end in '-aceae' to match the family

questions.q: In botanical nomenclature, what do specific epithets ending in '-ii' or '-yi' (such as Phlox hoodii or Danthonia parryi) typically indicate?
options: They reflect the name of the botanist, European explorer, or settler who 'discovered' or named the plant
They indicate that the plant is poisonous to herbivores and pollinators
They are traditional Cree or Indigenous names translated directly into Latin
They signify that the plant has a biennial or annual life cycle

questions.q: What are the five different regional or cultural names for the berry species known in Western Canada as 'Saskatoon'?
options: misaskwatomina (Cree), Saskatoon (Western Canada), June Berry, Service Berry (USA), and Rock Pear (translated from German)
Pin Cherry, Chokecherry, Buffaloberry, Crowberry, and Bearberry
Cloudberry, Salmonberry, Thimbleberry, Dewberry, and Loganberry
Huckleberry, Bilberry, Lingonberry, Cranberry, and Grouseberry

questions.q: What are the three main categories of information needed to thoroughly describe a plant species?
options: Environment (where, soil type/moisture, elevation), Vegetative Characteristics (form, branching, leaf arrangement/shape, surfaces, stipules, belowground organs), and Reproductive Characteristics (inflorescence, floral structure, fruits, seeds)
Only floral petal count, seed weight, and chromosome number
Market value, timber volume, and rotation age
Latitude, longitude, and UTM zone

questions.q: What do 'Plant Life Forms' classify, and how do they relate to phylogenetic relatedness (e.g., Cornus canadensis vs. Cornus florida)?
options: They classify plants by their function in the ecosystem and growth form (trees, shrubs, herbs/forbs/grasses, mosses); unrelated species can share the same life-form, and phylogenetically related species (like bunchberry Cornus canadensis and flowering dogwood Cornus florida) can have very different life-forms
They classify plants strictly by evolutionary genetics; two species in the same genus must always have the exact same growth form
They classify plants based solely on whether they have simple or compound leaves
They group plants by flower color and pollinator preference

questions.q: What is the basis of 'Raunkiaer's Life Forms' classification system?
options: The location of the plant's perennating buds (persistent meristems) during dormant or unfavorable seasons
The depth of the primary taproot in meters
The ratio of leaf length to leaf width
The number of cotyledons in the germinating seed

questions.q: In Raunkiaer's Life Forms, how are Phanerophytes, Chamaephytes, and Hemicryptophytes distinguished by the height/location of their perennating buds?
options: Phanerophyte: buds > 25 cm above the soil; Chamaephyte: buds < 25 cm above the soil; Hemicryptophyte: buds at or near the soil surface
Phanerophyte: buds submerged in water; Chamaephyte: buds > 10 meters high; Hemicryptophyte: annuals that survive only as seeds
Phanerophyte: buds below dry ground; Chamaephyte: buds on aerial epiphytes; Hemicryptophyte: buds > 25 cm above soil
All three have their perennating buds buried deep underground in bulbs or corms

questions.q: In Raunkiaer's Life Forms, what are Cryptophytes (and their तीन subtypes: Geophytes, Helophytes, Hydrophytes), Epiphytes, and Therophytes?
options: Cryptophytes have buds below soil or water—divided into Geophytes (buried in dry ground), Helophytes (in marsh/wetland mud), and Hydrophytes (submerged in water); Epiphytes grow on other plants with no connection to soil; Therophytes are annuals that survive unfavorable seasons as seeds
Geophytes are submerged water plants; Hydrophytes live in dry desert soil; Therophytes are tall woody trees
Cryptophytes have buds > 25 cm in the air; Epiphytes are marsh plants; Therophytes are perennial shrubs
Helophytes are annual desert herbs; Geophytes have no connection to the soil

questions.q: Compare Xylem and Phloem in terms of transport direction, cell vitality at maturity, cell types, and position within a vascular bundle:
options: Xylem moves water and minerals unidirectionally (roots to shoots) via lignified cells dead at maturity (tracheids, vessel elements) on the inside of the vascular bundle; Phloem moves water and nutrients bidirectionally via live cells (sieve tube elements with cytoplasm and perforated cell walls) on the outer side of the vascular bundle
Xylem moves sugars bidirectionally via live cells on the outside of the bundle; Phloem moves water unidirectionally via dead lignified cells on the inside
Both xylem and phloem are dead at maturity and transport fluids strictly downward from shoots to roots
Xylem is located in the epidermis, while phloem is located exclusively in the root cap

questions.q: In primary root growth, what are the functions of the 'Endodermis' and the 'Pericycle'?
options: The endodermis is a hydrophobic layer of cells that regulates water and nutrient uptake into the vascular cylinder; the pericycle consists of cells located between the phloem and endodermis that can divide to form lateral roots
The endodermis is the outer root cap that secretes mucilage; the pericycle is the dead core of secondary wood
The endodermis produces root hairs on the exterior of the root; the pericycle conducts sugars to the leaves
Both layers are photosynthetic tissues found only in aerial stems

questions.q: What are the two main root growth strategies (and their variations), and what are the specialized functions of Contractile, Tuberous, Buttress, Anchor, and Haustorial roots?
options: The two main strategies are Diffuse (shallow diffuse, fibrous diffuse, diffuse with adventitious roots) and Tap (branched shallow taproot, deep taproot); Specializations: Contractile (dandelion), Tuberous (beet), Buttress (thin, nutrient-poor tropical soil), Anchor (eroding soil), and Haustoria (parasitic plants like mistletoe Arceuthobium americanum that grow into host vascular bundles)
The two main strategies are Haustorial and Aerial; Buttress roots only occur in arctic tundra, and Contractile roots only occur in mistletoe
Taproots grow from stem nodes in corn, whereas Fibrous roots are single enlarged storage roots in carrots
Haustoria are nitrogen-fixing root nodules found in carrots and dandelions

questions.q: In a developing shoot, what are 'Axillary Meristems' and what subtends them?
options: Regions of meristematic tissue on the sides of the developing shoot that produce lateral buds on nodes (separated by internodes); they are generally dormant but can activate to form a branch, and are subtended by an axillary leaf
The primary root cap meristems that are subtended by root hairs
Dead sclerenchyma caps that permanently prevent lateral branches from forming
Lateral meristems (cork cambium) that only produce outer bark

questions.q: What are 'Buds' on a woody stem, and how are 'Foliate (Naked)', 'Valvate', and 'Imbricated' buds distinguished?
options: Buds are immature (compressed) branches with miniature leaves or flowers; Foliate (naked) buds have no bud scales (leaf structure is observable); Valvate buds have bud scales that meet at the edges without overlapping; Imbricated buds have overlapping bud scales
Foliate buds have overlapping scales; Valvate buds have no scales; Imbricated buds have scales that do not overlap
All buds are underground storage organs covered in suberized pericycle
Valvate buds only occur on roots, while Imbricated buds lack an apical meristem

questions.q: How do you distinguish a true 'Terminal Bud' from a 'Lateral (Axial) Bud' on a winter twig, and what happens in species that lack a true terminal bud?
options: A true terminal bud forms at the end of the twig (denoting the end of the present year's growth) and has NO leaf scar beneath it, whereas lateral buds form at the base of a leaf (above a leaf scar); in species without a true terminal bud, a tip-scar is present and the nearest lateral bud takes the place of a terminal bud (pseudoterminal)
A true terminal bud always sits directly above a large heart-shaped leaf scar, whereas lateral buds have no leaf scars
Terminal buds are found along the internodes, while lateral buds form rings around the base of the trunk
Only coniferous trees have lateral buds; deciduous trees only have terminal buds

questions.q: How can you determine the age of segments on a winter woody twig, and what features on the stem and leaf scars assist in winter twig identification?
options: Rings of terminal bud scale scars mark the end of each previous year's growth (allowing you to count back 1 year ago, 2 years ago, etc.); leaf scar size/shape, bundle scar number and pattern, and raised corky lenticels are key traits for winter twig ID
Each individual lenticel represents one full year of twig growth
Bundle scars fall off every autumn and cannot be seen on winter twigs
Leaf scars are randomly arranged and never match the arrangement of lateral buds

questions.q: Compare 'Monopodial' and 'Sympodial' branching patterns (including Monochasium and Dichasium), and explain why sympodial branching is ecologically advantageous in Willows (Salix sp.):
options: In Monopodial branching, 1 apical bud is responsible for height growth with a dominant main axis and cone-shaped crown (e.g., spruce); in Sympodial branching, the initial apical meristem is short-lived and lateral branches elongate the stem (Monochasium if 1 lateral branch dominates; Dichasium if opposite/decussate branches grow equally), making it well adapted to recover from disturbances like fire, flooding, and herbivory
Monopodial branching has no dominant main axis and forms a rounded shrub; Sympodial branching has a single permanent apical bud and a strict cone-shaped crown
Monochasium has two opposite branches growing equally, whereas Dichasium has a single dominant lateral branch
Sympodial plants die immediately if their terminal bud is browsed by herbivores

questions.q: What do the botanical terms 'Caulescent', 'Cauline', and 'Acaulescent' mean?
options: Caulescent: having an obvious leafy above-ground stem (e.g., willows); Cauline: belonging or referring to the stem (e.g., cauline leaves or cauline hairs); Acaulescent: appearing to lack a stem (or having a very short stem) with leaves appearing strictly basal (e.g., dandelion / false dandelion)
Caulescent: lacking a stem; Cauline: referring to root hairs; Acaulescent: having a tall woody trunk
All three terms refer to aquatic plants with submerged leaves
Cauline leaves are positioned exclusively in a basal rosette at the ground surface

questions.q: How do 'Rhizomes' and 'Stolons' enable clonal growth, how do they differ from roots, and what do 'Genet', 'Ramet', and 'Caespitose' mean?
options: Rhizomes (belowground) and Stolons/runners (aboveground) are modified horizontal stems with nodes, internodes, and leaves; a Genet is the entire connected clonal colony of genetically identical individuals, while a Ramet is an individual unit within the genet; Caespitose describes clonal plants (often monocots like bunchgrasses) with very short rhizomes resulting in densely tufted forms
Rhizomes are aboveground runners and Stolons are belowground roots lacking nodes; a Ramet is the whole colony and a Genet is a single shoot; Caespitose means widely spreading by long stolons
Genets are genetically diverse seedlings produced by sexual reproduction, whereas Ramets are parasitic haustoria
Caespitose refers exclusively to tall single-trunked coniferous trees

questions.q: Botanically, what is a 'Flower', and what are its four terminal whorls?
options: A flower is a short determinate (compressed) shoot bearing highly modified leaves (foliar appendages) arranged in four terminal whorls: two sterile whorls (sepals and petals) and two fertile whorls of sporophylls (microsporophylls/stamens and megasporophylls/carpels)
A flower is an indeterminate root structure composed of four whorls of suberized cork scales
A flower is an elongated internode bearing two fertile whorls (sepals and petals) and two sterile whorls (stamens and pistils)
A flower is a vegetative bud that never stops elongating its main axis

questions.q: What is the fundamental difference between an 'Indeterminate Inflorescence' and a 'Determinate Inflorescence'?
options: In an Indeterminate inflorescence, the youngest flower occurs at the end/center of the main axis (rachis) as the terminal bud continues producing new flowers; in a Determinate inflorescence, the oldest flower terminates the main axis as the terminal bud stops growing and new lateral flowers form from axillary buds
In an Indeterminate inflorescence, the oldest flower is at the tip of the main axis; in a Determinate inflorescence, the youngest flower is at the tip
Indeterminate inflorescences bear only a single solitary flower, while Determinate inflorescences never open
Determinate inflorescences only occur in wind-pollinated gymnosperms

questions.q: In an inflorescence, what are the 'Peduncle', 'Rachis', 'Pedicel', 'Bract', and 'Involucre'?
options: Peduncle: main supporting stalk of the entire inflorescence; Rachis: main central axis above the peduncle; Pedicel: stalk of an individual flower; Bract: modified leaf at the base of a flower/inflorescence; Involucre: a cluster or whorl of bracts subtending an inflorescence
Pedicel: main stalk of the whole inflorescence; Peduncle: stalk of a single flower; Involucre: the petal whorl of a solitary flower
Rachis: the stalk attaching a simple leaf to the stem; Bract: the vascular bundle inside a root
Involucre: a fleshy spike of unisexual flowers; Peduncle: a sessile flower lacking a stalk

questions.q: Compare the four basic inflorescence types: 'Solitary', 'Spike', 'Raceme', and 'Panicle':
options: Solitary: a single flower on a stem; Spike: unbranched inflorescence with sessile (unstalked) flowers; Raceme: unbranched inflorescence with stalked flowers on pedicels; Panicle: a branched (compound) raceme
Spike: branched inflorescence with stalked flowers; Raceme: unbranched inflorescence with sessile flowers; Panicle: a single solitary flower
Raceme: flat-topped cluster arising from one point; Spike: coiled one-sided cyme
All four types have sessile flowers attached directly to a fleshy spadix

questions.q: How do the three flat-topped (or convex) inflorescences—'Corymb', 'Cyme', and 'Umbel'—differ in structure and flower maturation?
options: Corymb: indeterminate flat-topped inflorescence with pedicels of unequal length arising along the rachis and youngest flowers in the center/end; Cyme: determinate flat-topped inflorescence with the oldest flower terminating the center/end of the main axis; Umbel: flat-topped inflorescence where all pedicels arise from a single common point
Corymb: oldest flower in the center; Cyme: all pedicels arise from a single common point; Umbel: unbranched spike with sessile flowers
All three are determinate inflorescences with sessile flowers along an elongated axis
An Umbel has pedicels attached at different heights along a central rachis

questions.q: What is a 'Scorpioid Cyme' and which plant families is it typical of? What is a 'Compound Umbel' (with rays, umbellets, involucre, and involucels) and which family is it typical of?
options: A Scorpioid cyme is a determinate cyme with one-sided branching forming a coiled inflorescence, typical of Boraginaceae and Hydrophyllaceae; a Compound umbel has primary rays arising from a common point (subtended by an involucre of bracts), each bearing a secondary umbellet of pedicels (subtended by an involucel of bractlets), typical of the carrot family (Apiaceae / Umbelliferae)
A Scorpioid cyme is typical of the carrot family (Apiaceae); a Compound umbel is a coiled one-sided inflorescence typical of Boraginaceae
An umbellet is the main supporting stalk of a simple cyme, and an involucel is a modified root
Compound umbels have sessile flowers arranged on a pendulous catkin

questions.q: Compare the specialized inflorescences 'Spadix' (and its 'Spathe') and 'Catkin (Ament)', including the plant groups they characterize:
options: Spadix: a thick, fleshy spike of unisexual, apetalous flowers (male clustered above female) surrounded by a vase/funnel-like modified leaf called a spathe, characteristic of the Arum family (Araceae, e.g., Calla palustris); Catkin (Ament): a spike-like, often pendulous inflorescence of unisexual, apetalous flowers typical of willow (Salix), cottonwood (Populus), oak (Quercus), alder (Alnus), and birch (Betula) (formerly grouped as Amentiferae)
Spadix: a pendulous wind-pollinated catkin found on willows and oaks; Catkin: a fleshy spike surrounded by a brightly colored spathe in the Arum family
Both Spadix and Catkin consist of large, showy bisexual flowers with four whorls of petals
A spathe is the woody cone scale of a pine tree, and an ament is a solitary lily flower

questions.q: What distinguishes a 'Simple Leaf' from a 'Compound Leaf', and how do you tell a leaflet (pinna) apart from a simple leaf on a stem?
options: A simple leaf has a single undivided blade, whereas a compound leaf has its blade divided into separate leaflets (pinnae) attached to a central axis (rachis); an axillary bud is present in the axil at the base of the main petiole of a simple or compound leaf, but never at the base of individual leaflets
Each individual leaflet of a compound leaf has its own axillary bud and stipules at its base on the rachis
Simple leaves are attached to a rachis, whereas compound leaves lack a petiole
Compound leaves only occur in monocots like grasses

questions.q: In the Key to Common Types of Leaf Divisions, how are Palmate, Ternate (Trifoliate), Biternate, and Triternate compound leaves defined?
options: Palmate: leaflets arise from a common point like fingers of a hand (if 3 leaflets = Ternate/Trifoliate; if >3 = Palmate); if the leaflets are further divided into secondary leaflets (decompound), twice divided = Biternate and thrice divided = Triternate
Palmate: leaflets arise from opposite sides of an elongated rachis; Biternate: a simple leaf with two lobes
Ternate leaves have 10 leaflets arranged in pairs ending in a tendril
Triternate means three simple leaves whorled at a single stem node

questions.q: In Pinnately compound leaves (where leaflets arise from opposite sides of an elongated rachis), how are Even-pinnate, Tendril-pinnate, Odd-pinnate (Imparipinnate), Bipinnate, and Tripinnate defined?
options: Even-pinnate (abruptly pinnate): even number of leaflets not ending in a tendril; Tendril-pinnate: even number of leaflets with the leaf ending in a tendril; Odd-pinnate (imparipinnate): odd number of leaflets with a terminal leaflet (if 3 leaflets = Ternate/Trifoliate); Decompound pinnate: twice divided = Bipinnate, thrice divided = Tripinnate
Odd-pinnate has an even number of leaflets ending in a tendril; Even-pinnate has a single terminal leaflet
Bipinnate means a simple leaf with two stipules; Tripinnate means leaflets arising from a single palmate point
Imparipinnate leaves have no rachis and attach directly to the root collar

questions.q: In the Key to Common Leaf Arrangements, define Basal, Cauline, Alternate, Distichous, Opposite, Decussate, and Whorled:
options: Basal: leaves at the base of the stem; Cauline: leaves on an elongated stem; Alternate: 1 leaf per node (Distichous = alternate leaves arranged in 2 flat opposite ranks); Opposite: 2 leaves per node (Decussate = opposite pairs rotated 90° at successive nodes); Whorled: 3 or more leaves per node
Alternate: 2 leaves per node; Opposite: 1 leaf per node; Whorled: leaves only at the base of the stem
Decussate means 1 leaf per node in a spiral; Distichous means 5 or more leaves per node
Basal leaves are borne high on the canopy branches, while Cauline leaves are underground scales

questions.q: Match the narrower Leaf Shapes—Acicular, Linear, Oblong, Lanceolate, Oblanceolate, Elliptic, and Oval—with their botanical definitions:
options: Acicular: needlelike; Linear: long and narrow with parallel sides; Oblong: ~3x as long as wide with nearly parallel sides; Lanceolate: lance-shaped (~4x as long as wide, widest near base); Oblanceolate: inversely lanceolate (widest near tip); Elliptic: outline of an ellipse (~2x as long as wide); Oval: broadly elliptic
Acicular: kidney-shaped; Linear: heart-shaped; Lanceolate: perfectly circular; Elliptic: needlelike
Lanceolate is widest at the apex, whereas Oblanceolate is widest at the base
Oblong leaves are 10 times wider than they are long

questions.q: Match the broader/lobed Leaf Shapes—Ovate, Obovate, Reniform, and Cordate—with their botanical definitions:
options: Ovate: egg-shaped in outline (widest below the middle toward the base); Obovate: inversely ovate (widest above the middle toward the tip); Reniform: kidney-shaped; Cordate: heart-shaped
Ovate: widest near the tip; Obovate: widest near the base; Reniform: needlelike; Cordate: linear
Reniform is lance-shaped, and Cordate is kidney-shaped
All four shapes have parallel sides and are at least 6 times as long as wide

questions.q: How are the five Leaf Base shapes—Obtuse, Acute, Cuneate, Oblique, and Cordate—defined?
options: Obtuse: rounded base; Acute: coming to a point; Cuneate: wedge-shaped, coming to a sharp narrow point; Oblique: asymmetrical base where the two sides of the leaf blade intersect the midrib at different points; Cordate: heart-shaped (notched) base
Oblique: symmetrical rounded base; Cuneate: heart-shaped notched base; Cordate: wedge-shaped base
Obtuse bases come to a sharp bristle-like point, while Acute bases are flat and cut-off
All five terms describe the outer margin teeth rather than the base of the blade

questions.q: How are the six Leaf Tip (Apex) shapes—Acute, Acuminate, Obtuse, Truncate, Emarginate, and Cuspidate—defined?
options: Acute: sharp-pointed; Acuminate: gradually tapered to a drawn-out long point; Obtuse: rounded; Truncate: flat, appearing squared or cut-off at the tip; Emarginate: having a shallow notch at the tip; Cuspidate: coming abruptly to a sharp, rigid, bristle-like tip (cusp)
Truncate: tapering to a long point; Emarginate: coming to a sharp bristle; Cuspidate: notched at the apex
Acuminate: flat and cut-off; Obtuse: sharp-pointed; Acute: deeply notched
Emarginate means the leaf margin has no teeth, and Truncate means kidney-shaped

questions.q: Compare the nine Leaf Margin types: Entire, Undulate, Sinuate, Serrate, Dentate, Crenate, Lobed, Cleft, and Parted:
options: Entire: smooth margin without teeth or lobes; Undulate: slightly wavy; Sinuate: strongly wavy; Serrate: saw-toothed with sharp teeth pointing forward toward the apex; Dentate: sharp teeth pointing outward at right angles; Crenate: rounded/scalloped teeth; Lobed, Cleft, and Parted: margins incised to progressively deeper depths toward the midrib
Entire: deeply cut to the midrib; Serrate: smooth without teeth; Crenate: sharp spines pointing backward
Dentate teeth point forward toward the tip, whereas Serrate teeth are rounded scallops
Undulate means divided into separate leaflets, and Sinuate means covered in waxy bloom

questions.q: Match the eight Leaf Surface ('Hairdo') terms—Glabrous, Ciliate, Pubescent, Strigose, Villous, Tomentose, Glandular, and Glaucous—with their exact definitions:
options: Glabrous: smooth, no hairs present; Ciliate: only the margin fringed with hairs; Pubescent: covered with short, soft hairs; Strigose: covered with appressed, fine, straight hairs; Villous: covered with long, soft, usually curved hairs; Tomentose: densely matted, woolly hairs; Glandular: hairs bearing secretory glands; Glaucous: covered with a bluish-white or bluish-gray waxy bloom
Glabrous: densely matted hairs; Glaucous: covered in sharp stiff bristles; Tomentose: completely hairless and smooth
Strigose: long curly hairs; Villous: flat appressed straight hairs; Ciliate: covered in a bluish waxy bloom
Pubescent means lacking hairs, and Glandular means the leaf blade is divided into leaflets

questions.q: What are the primary modes of asexual reproduction in plants?
options: Vegetative reproduction (via root/leaf plantlets, modified stems, or floral plantlets) and apomixis (clonal seed production without fertilization)
Meiotic division of megaspores and microspores within strobili
Double fertilization yielding a diploid zygote and triploid endosperm
Fusion of flagellated sperm cells inside water droplets on archegonia

questions.q: What are vegetative plantlets (such as root suckers in trembling aspen or stump sprouts in birch), and what are the resulting individual stems termed?
options: Adventitious shoots and roots originating from newly formed buds along stems or roots (often following disturbance); each individual is a ramet belonging to a clonal genet
Haploid gametophytic thalli arising directly from unfertilized ovules; each individual is a spore
Specialized floral bracts that secrete sweet nectar; each individual is a nectary spur
Lignified modified leaves that enclose the terminal bud during winter dormancy

questions.q: How do Auxins and Cytokinins interact to regulate 'Apical Dominance' in plant shoots?
options: Auxins (synthesized in apical meristems) move downward to inhibit lateral bud growth; Cytokinins (synthesized primarily in roots) promote cell division and bud break when auxin flow is disrupted
Auxins promote the breaking and elongation of lateral buds; Cytokinins inhibit lateral growth and enforce dormancy
Both auxins and cytokinins are synthesized strictly in the flower petals to attract biotic pollinators
Auxins mobilize through the xylem to stimulate root suckering, while cytokinins are released from bud scales

questions.q: What occurs when the flow of auxin from the shoot tip to lateral buds is disrupted (e.g., by fire, mechanical decapitation, or herbivory)?
options: Apical dominance is removed, allowing root-derived cytokinins to activate and promote the rapid growth of lateral buds
The entire plant immediately enters terminal senescence and sheds all lateral branches
The roots cease all cell division and stop absorbing soil water and minerals
The plant is forced to switch permanently to obligate sexual reproduction via catkins

questions.q: How do modified horizontal stems (Rhizomes and Stolons) differ from true roots?
options: Rhizomes (belowground) and stolons/runners (aboveground) possess nodes, internodes, axillary buds, and scale leaves just like aerial stems
Rhizomes and stolons lack nodes, internodes, and vascular tissue entirely
Rhizomes and stolons are covered in root caps and absorb water through root hairs
They originate strictly from the pericycle layer inside the stele

questions.q: What are the botanical definitions of 'Bulb', 'Corm', and 'Tuber'?
options: Bulb: underground bud with thick, fleshy leaf scales; Corm: short, solid, vertically oriented inflated stem with papery leaves; Tuber: thickened portion of a rhizome (or inflated underground stem) bearing nodes and buds
Bulb: an enlarged fibrous root; Corm: a horizontal aerial stolon; Tuber: an unbranched flower spike
Bulb: a solid stem core without scales; Corm: a cluster of fleshy roots; Tuber: a parasitic haustorium
All three are modified reproductive flowers that produce clonal seeds via apomixis

questions.q: What ecological advantage do thick belowground storage organs (bulbs, corms, tubers, rhizomes) provide to perennial plants?
options: They serve as adaptations to stressful environments (cold or arid climates) and allow early spring emergence ahead of competitors
They eliminate the need for cellular respiration by storing pressurized atmospheric oxygen
They produce fragrant volatile essential oils that deter burrowing rodents
They allow plants to absorb nutrients without establishing mycorrhizal associations

questions.q: What is 'Epiphylly' and how does it differ from 'Micropropagation'?
options: Epiphylly is the natural development of plantlets from non-flowering vegetative tissues (such as leaves); Micropropagation is the artificial lab culturing of whole plants from small tissue explants
Epiphylly is the tissue culture of roots in test tubes; Micropropagation is the natural formation of aerial runners
Epiphylly refers to wind pollination; Micropropagation refers to insect pollination
Epiphylly is seed development without fertilization; Micropropagation is spore dispersal

questions.q: What is the distinction between 'False Vivipary' and 'True Vivipary' in plants?
options: False vivipary: floral or seed structures are replaced by vegetative plantlets, bulbils, or tillers; True vivipary: seeds undergo precocious germination while still attached to the parent plant (e.g., mangroves)
False vivipary occurs only in gymnosperm cones; True vivipary occurs only in desert cacti
False vivipary involves embryo production via fertilization; True vivipary is vegetative propagation by stolons
False vivipary produces diploid seeds, while True vivipary produces haploid spores

questions.q: What is 'Apomixis' and in which plant families is it especially prevalent?
options: Asexual (clonal) seed production where the embryo develops without meiosis or fertilization, producing seeds genetically identical to the maternal parent; common in Asteraceae, Rosaceae, and Poaceae
The rapid production of adventitious root suckers following fire; common in Salicaceae and Pinaceae
The shedding of floral bud scales prior to anthesis; common in Araceae and Ericaceae
The cross-pollination of flowers by nocturnal moths and bats; common in Orchidaceae

questions.q: How does vegetative propagation occur via 'Layering', 'Air Rooting', and 'Fragmentation'?

questions.q: What comprises the 'Androecium' and what occurs within the anther microsporangia?

questions.q: Match the major Placentation types—Axile, Parietal, Free-Central, Marginal, Basal, and Apical—with their structural positions inside the ovary:

questions.q: What do the floral condition terms 'Complete', 'Incomplete', 'Bisexual (Perfect)', and 'Unisexual (Imperfect)' describe?

questions.q: How are the sexual conditions 'Monoecious', 'Dioecious', and 'Polygamous' defined in plants?

questions.q: What is a 'Hypanthium' and how does it relate to flower insertion terms?

questions.q: Compare the three types of floral insertion: 'Hypogynous', 'Perigynous', and 'Epigynous':

questions.q: How are the floral symmetry classes—'Actinomorphic', 'Zygomorphic', and 'Asymmetric'—defined?

questions.q: In floral morphology, what is the precise difference between 'Connate' and 'Adnate' fusion of parts?

questions.q: What do the terms 'Distinct' and 'Free' mean when describing unfused floral organs?

questions.q: What is a 'Caryopsis' (grain) and which family does it characterize?

questions.q: What is a 'Multiple Fruit' (such as a pineapple or a fig syconium)?

options: Persistent styles can form feathery plumes (Rosaceae and Ranunculaceae, e.g., Geum triflorum); persistent sepals can form a wind-dispersal pappus (dandelions, Asteraceae) or an inflated, protective papery husk (tomatillo, Solanaceae)

Persistent anthers secrete nectar to attract ants that bury the whole branch underground
Persistent bud scales transform the fruit into a photosynthetic succulent stem

questions.q: What is the primary evolutionary purpose of fruits, and why is seed dispersal critical for plant survival?
options: To disperse seeds away from the parent plant; dispersal colonizes new environments, reduces resource competition with parent plants, and reduces the chance that predators destroy all of a plant's yearly seed crop
To provide food for human agricultural consumption and prevent soil erosion
To permanently lock seeds inside the soil to prevent them from germinating during warm years
To absorb atmospheric nitrogen and convert it directly into protein reserves

questions.q: What is a 'Diaspore' and what four primary dispersal mechanisms do diaspores utilize?
options: The plant dispersal unit (seed, fruit, or even entire inflorescences/plants like tumbleweeds); dispersed via Passive dispersal (gravity), Wind dispersal (wings, pappus, tumbling), Water dispersal (floating), and Animal dispersal (endozoochory, caching, external attachment)
The fungal mantle surrounding mycorrhizal roots; dispersed via apoplastic and symplastic flow
The dormant shoot apical meristem; dispersed by terminal bud scale abscission
A specialized underground corm; dispersed exclusively by subterranean earthworms

questions.q: What is 'Endozoochory' and how does an animal's digestive tract affect the seeds of fleshy fruits (e.g., chokecherry, Prunus virginiana)?
options: Dispersal of seeds through ingestion by animals; animals eat the fleshy pericarp, and passage through the digestive system scarifies the seed coat, aiding germination after defecation
External attachment of barbed fruits to animal fur and bird feathers
The caching and burial of hard-shelled nuts by squirrels and jays
The consumption of pollen grains by bee larvae inside the hive

questions.q: What is 'Temporal Dispersal' in plant populations, and what did the famous Beal Seed Experiment (started in 1879) demonstrate?
options: The dispersal of seeds across time rather than space by forming a dormant soil seed bank; the Beal experiment showed that buried seeds of certain weedy species remain viable and germinate after more than 140 years in the soil
The ability of tree branches to delay producing annual rings during drought years
The rapid timing of explosive seed ejection within milliseconds of touching the pod
The synchronous flowering of bamboo species every 60 to 120 years across continents

questions.q: How do diaspores of certain grasses and herbs (such as needle-and-thread grass Hesperostipa curtiseta, porcupine grass Stipa spartea, and stork's bill Erodium cicutarium) achieve 'Self-Burial' in soil?
options: They possess hygroscopically active, bent/twisted awns or styles that coil and uncoil with changes in humidity, physically drilling the pointed diaspore into cracks in the soil
They secrete digestive acids from the seed coat that melt through solid rock and clay
They rely on contractile roots that pull the diaspore downward into deep soil horizons
They produce underground stolons that pull the seed downward immediately after pollination

questions.q: What is 'Phylogeny' and how is it typically represented in modern biological systematics?
options: The evolutionary history of a species, group of organisms, or specific feature; typically expressed as a phylogenetic tree (or cladogram) showing inferred evolutionary relationships
A static classification of plants based strictly on flower color and commercial market value
The developmental sequence of a single seed germinating into a mature flowering plant
The process of creating artificial hybrids through greenhouse cross-pollination

questions.q: In phylogenetic terminology, what is an 'Apomorphy' and what is a 'Synapomorphy'?
options: An apomorphy is an evolutionary novel trait derived from an ancestral form; a synapomorphy is an apomorphy shared among related taxa inherited from a common ancestor
An apomorphy is an ancestral primitive trait; a synapomorphy is a convergent trait that evolved independently
An apomorphy is a fertile reproductive flower; a synapomorphy is a vegetative leaf sucker
Both terms describe non-vascular moss gametophytes lacking xylem and phloem

questions.q: What is the 'APG IV' system published in 2016, and how does it organize higher ranks of land plants?
options: A modern, mostly molecular-based system of plant taxonomy that avoids ranks above the order; all land plants were placed in the class Equisitopsida and divided into 16 subclasses (including Magnoliidae for flowering plants)
The original 1735 morphological classification system authored by Carl Linnaeus in Systema Naturae
A manual forestry grading scale that groups trees into pulpwood, sawtimber, and veneer logs
A system that groups all spore-bearing pteridophytes into the single family Asteraceae

questions.q: In the standard taxonomic hierarchy for plants, what standardized Latin suffixes correspond to Division, Class, Subclass, Order, Family, and Subfamily?

Division: -ales; Class: -aceae; Subclass: -ophyta; Order: -opsida; Family: -idae; Subfamily: -um
Division: -idae; Class: -oideae; Subclass: -ales; Order: -aceae; Family: -opsida; Subfamily: -ophyta
Division: -aceae; Class: -idae; Subclass: -opsida; Order: -ophyta; Family: -ales; Subfamily: -oideae

questions.q: What is the definition of a 'Taxon' (plural: 'Taxa') in biological classification?
options: A convenient term applied to any formal taxonomic group at any rank (e.g., species, genus, family, division)
The specific Latin epithet used exclusively for naming cultivated agricultural varieties
The name of the original author or botanist who discovered the plant specimen
A cluster of sporangia covered by a protective flap of leaf tissue

questions.q: Under the Arthur Cronquist taxonomic system, how are the non-vascular plants (Bryophytes) and vascular spore-makers (Pteridophytes) grouped by division?
options: Non-vascular: Anthocerotophyta (hornworts), Hepatophyta (liverworts), Bryophyta (mosses); Spore-making vascular (Pteridophytes): Lycopodiophyta, Equisetophyta, Psilophyta, Polypodiophyta
Non-vascular: Coniferophyta and Cycadophyta; Spore-making vascular: Magnoliophyta and Liliopsida
Non-vascular: Magnoliopsida and Liliidae; Spore-making vascular: Pinaceae and Cupressaceae
All non-vascular and seedless vascular plants are grouped into the single division Spermatophyta

questions.q: Under the Cronquist system, how are the Seed-Making Divisions (Superdivision Spermatophyta) divided between cone-bearing and flower-bearing plants?
options: Cone-bearing: Coniferophyta (Pinophyta), Cycadophyta, Ginkgophyta, Gnetophyta; Flower-bearing: Magnoliophyta (Class Liliopsida = monocots, Class Magnoliopsida = dicots)
Cone-bearing: Magnoliophyta; Flower-bearing: Lycopodiophyta and Equisetophyta
Cone-bearing: Bryophyta and Hepatophyta; Flower-bearing: Pteridophyta and Psilophyta
Cone-bearing: Liliopsida; Flower-bearing: Ginkgophyta and Cycadophyta

questions.q: What morphological and anatomical characteristics define the 'Bryophytes' (non-vascular plants)?
options: They lack vascular tissue (xylem and phloem), true roots, flowers, and seeds; their stem- and leaf-like structures are simple and thin to allow direct surface absorption of water
They possess well-developed secondary xylem and thick, suberized root barks
They reproduce via large woody megastrobili with winged seeds
They have reticulate megaphyll fronds that unroll from fiddleheads

questions.q: What is the ONLY unique defining diagnostic characteristic of all vascular plants (Tracheophyta / Tracheobionta)?
options: The presence of specialized vascular transport systems (xylem and phloem tissues)
The production of flowers and enclosed ovary fruits
The formation of seeds and pollen tubes
The presence of an external waxy cuticle covering every vegetative organ

questions.q: Which of the following characteristics are common to some, BUT NOT ALL, vascular plants?
options: Waxy cuticle covering the epidermis, differentiation into true stems, leaves, and roots, an independent and structurally dominant sporophyte, and high volume-to-surface-area ratios
Vascular bundles containing conducting xylem and phloem elements
Cell division via apical meristems producing primary growth
Alternation of multicellular generations during the reproductive cycle

questions.q: On the vascular plant cladogram, what evolutionary innovation separates the Euphyllophyta (ferns, horsetails, seed plants) from the Lycopodiophyta (clubmosses, spikemosses, quillworts)?
options: The evolution of true leaves (megaphylls with branched vascular tissue and leaf gaps)
The evolution of vascular xylem and phloem tissues
The transition from aquatic habitats onto dry land
The development of woody cones (strobili) bearing ovules

questions.q: What defining reproductive traits characterize the 'Pteridophytes' (seedless vascular plants)?
options: They disperse via haploid spores produced in sporangia, produce free-living (usually photosynthetic and exosporic) gametophytes, possess motile swimming sperm, and require liquid water for fertilization
They reproduce via double fertilization to form an embryo and triploid endosperm inside a seed
They produce naked seeds exposed on the surface of woody ovuliferous cone scales
Their dominant generation is the haploid gametophyte, while the sporophyte is completely dependent

questions.q: How does an 'Eusporangiate' fern differ from a 'Leptosporangiate' fern in development and spore production?
options: Eusporangiate: large sporangia develop from several initial cells producing many spores (sometimes fused into synangia; e.g., Equisetaceae); Leptosporangiate: small sporangia develop from a single initial cell producing a small, definite number (<128) of spores in sori (e.g., Polypodiaceae)
Eusporangiate: sporangia develop from a single cell producing <128 spores; Leptosporangiate: sporangia develop from multiple epidermal cells
Eusporangiate ferns produce seeds, whereas Leptosporangiate ferns produce motile swimming sperm
Eusporangiate sporangia are covered by a papery indusium, whereas Leptosporangiate sporangia lack any covering

questions.q: In the pteridophyte phylogeny, which lineages are Eusporangiate versus Leptosporangiate?
options: Eusporangiate: Psilotales (whisk ferns), Ophioglossales (grapeferns), Equisetales (horsetails), and Marattiales; Leptosporangiate: Osmundales, Hymenophyllales, Gleicheniales, Schizaeales, Salviniales, Cyatheales, and Polypodiales
Eusporangiate: Polypodiaceae and tree ferns; Leptosporangiate: horsetails and whisk ferns
All ferns are leptosporangiate except for the gymnosperms and angiosperms
Lycophytes are leptosporangiate, while all true ferns are eusporangiate

questions.q: What is the difference between 'Homosporous' and 'Heterosporous' plants?
options: Homosporous: all spores are identical in size and form, producing bisexual (monoicous) gametophytes bearing both antheridia and archegonia; Heterosporous: produce two distinct spore types (megaspores -> female megagametophyte; microspores -> male microgametophyte)
Homosporous plants produce seeds, while heterosporous plants produce unbranched rhizomes
Homosporous plants have male and female flowers on separate plants (dioecious); Heterosporous plants are strictly monoecious
Heterosporous plants disperse spores by explosive dehiscence, while homosporous plants disperse via water currents

questions.q: How do 'Microphylls' and 'Megaphylls' differ structurally and vascularly in pteridophytes?
options: Microphylls: usually small (awn- or scale-like) with a single unbranched vein superficially connected to the stem vascular system; Megaphylls (fronds): usually large leaves with branched/reticulate veins, a direct gap in the stem vascular system, and development by unrolling

Microphylls are found only on seed plants; Megaphylls are found only on non-vascular mosses
Microphylls are reproductive petals, whereas Megaphylls are sterile roots

questions.q: What are the key morphological and evolutionary traits of the family Lycopodiaceae (clubmoss or ground pine family)?
options: Microphyllous leaves, homosporous reproduction with eusporangia in leaf axils (often clustered into terminal strobili), adventitious roots from rhizomes/stolons, dichotomously branching stems, and the longest continuous fossil record of any vascular plant (formed Carboniferous coal)
Megaphyllous fronds with sori, leptosporangiate sporangia, and seeds produced inside fleshy berries
Jointed, ridged stems with whorled branches and scale leaves connate into a nodal sheath
Non-vascular thalli producing haploid gemmae cups and swimming sperm

questions.q: What morphological characteristics are used to identify and distinguish species of Lycopodiaceae (such as Lycopodium annotinum, L. complanatum, and L. obscurum)?
options: Stem branching patterns (including runners/rhizomes), microphyll shape and presence of terminal awns/bristles, and the presence, stalk length, and arrangement of cones (strobili)
The number of petals and whether the flower ovary is superior or inferior
The type of fleshy fruit (berry, drupe, or pome) produced in autumn
The presence of Casparian strips and passage cells in the endodermis

questions.q: What famous ancient extinct tree-like lycophyte from the Carboniferous period grew up to 30 meters tall and contributed to major global coal deposits?
options: Lepidodendron
Equisetum arvense
Osmunda regalis
Dryopteris filix-mas

questions.q: What are the distinguishing vegetative and reproductive features of the family Equisetaceae (horsetails or scouring rushes, genus Equisetum)?
options: Perennial rhizomatous herbs of moist sites with jointed, ridged, hollow stems; reduced scale-like leaves connate into a toothed nodal sheath; eusporangia aggregated into terminal strobili ('cones'); ancient species had secondary growth (modern are herbaceous)
Large bipinnate fronds with round sori on the underside covered by umbrella-shaped indusia
Segmented succulent stems with sharp spines and yellow actinomorphic flowers
Non-vascular upright shoots bearing capsules that open by an operculum lid

questions.q: What key morphological traits are used to key out and identify different species within the genus Equisetum?
options: Presence or absence of whorled branches, length of nodal sheaths and number of sheath teeth, stem width/groove count, and whether cone tips are rounded or pointed (apiculate)
Petal color, stamen fusion, and nectary spur length
Bark thickness and annual ring counts in secondary xylem
Number of seeds inside the fleshy berry locule

questions.q: Why is the Royal Fern family (Osmundaceae, e.g., Osmunda regalis) historically considered an evolutionary intermediate between eusporangiate and leptosporangiate ferns?
options: They are large ferns often called 'flowering ferns' with striking leaf dimorphism (separate fertile sporangia-bearing fronds/pinnae and sterile photosynthetic fronds), whose sporangia develop from intermediate initial cell patterns; often indicate acidic peatland habitats
They produce true flowers with sepals and petals but disperse via naked gymnosperm seeds
They have microphyll leaves with single veins but possess woody secondary xylem like conifers
They lack vascular tissues entirely in their rhizomes but have complex megaphyll fronds

questions.q: In the family Polypodiaceae (and order Polypodiales), what are the anatomical terms for the fern leaf and its divisions?
options: Frond = entire fern leaf (Blade + Stipe/petiole); Pinna = primary division of a pinnate blade; Pinnule = ultimate division of a pinna; Costa = midrib of a pinna; Rachis = main axis of the blade; Fiddlehead (crozier) = young unrolling coiled leaf

questions.q: What is a 'Sorus' (plural: 'Sori') and what is an 'Indusium' in true ferns?

A sorus is a modified floral nectar spur; an indusium is the petal corolla tube

questions.q: What morphological variations can fern sori and indusia exhibit across different genera (e.g., Dryopteris, Polypodium, Pteris, Asplenium)?

All ferns have identical circular sori with fleshy hesperidium rinds
Sori only form inside subterranean corms and are protected by papery stipules
Fern sori develop strictly inside the female archegonium of the flower receptacle

questions.q: What anatomical features allow 'Tree Ferns' (order Cyatheales) to produce tall upright trunk-like stems despite lacking a true woody secondary vascular cambium?

Concentric annual rings of spring wood and summer wood produced by a bifacial vascular cambium
Enlarged contractile corms that stack vertically on top of each other over centuries
Continuous balloon-like inflation of cortical parenchyma cells through high hydrostatic turgor pressure

questions.q: What key morphological characters are used when keying out and identifying species in the Polypodiaceae (and related fern families)?

Number of sepals, petals, stamens, and carpels inside the flower bud
Seed coat thickness, endosperm protein percentage, and fruit pericarp layers
Whether the plant is monoecious or dioecious and whether it is pollinated by beetles or moths

questions.q: What remarkable physiological capability characterizes certain members of the Selaginellidae (spikemosses, e.g., Selaginella lepidophylla), earning them the common name 'Resurrection Plants'?

A sticky, sugary coating secreted by extrafloral nectaries

questions.q: In Coniferophyta megastrobili (ovulate cones), what tissues and ploidy levels compose the developing ovule prior to and following fertilization?

questions.q: How does gymnosperm fertilization and embryo nutrition differ from that of angiosperms?

Liquid water is required for flagellated sperm to swim across the bark from male to female cones

questions.q: What anatomical traits in xylem and phloem distinguish most gymnosperms from angiosperms?

questions.q: What are the general vegetative and reproductive characteristics of the family Pinaceae?

questions.q: How do 'Short Shoots' (spur shoots) and 'Long Shoots' differ in conifers such as Larix (larch) and Pinus?

questions.q: What unique morphological and anatomical characteristics define the family Taxaceae (Yews, e.g., Taxus brevifolia)?

questions.q: What morphological difference distinguishes the female reproductive structure of Taxus from that of Torreya in the family Taxaceae?
