They lack a primary cell wall entirely, relying on a rigid secondary wall
They have perfectly uniform, thin, isodiametric walls

questions.q: What is the primary function of collenchyma tissue within a plant?
options: It provides flexible support for both growing organs and mature organs, such as leaves and floral parts (e.g., celery strings)
It serves as the primary site of starch, oil, and tannin storage
It forms an impermeable outer dermal layer to prevent water loss
It actively conducts water and dissolved minerals from the roots to the shoots

questions.q: What are the defining characteristics of sclerenchyma tissue?
options: It consists of cells with thick, tough, secondary walls impregnated with lignin, and most are dead at maturity
It consists of thin-walled living cells with large vacuoles that actively divide to heal wounds
It consists of living cells with unevenly thickened primary walls that provide flexible support
It is a complex tissue made of multiple cell types functioning exclusively in sugar transport

questions.q: What are 'Sclereids' (stone cells)?
options: A reduced form of sclerenchyma cells with highly thickened, lignified walls, responsible for the gritty texture of pears and the hardness of nut shells
Elongated, flexible cells found in collenchyma tissue that provide support to celery stalks
Specialized parenchyma cells containing chloroplasts for photosynthesis
Living epidermal cells that secrete waxy cuticles to protect the plant surface

questions.q: What form of sclerenchyma cell is usually longer than it is wide, features a proportionately tiny central cavity (lumen), and is used commercially in textiles and ropes?
options: Fibers
Sclereids
Chlorenchyma
Aerenchyma

questions.q: What is the primary function of vascular tissues in plants?
options: To act as the main transport systems, comprising the xylem and phloem
To provide the outer protective covering of the entire plant
To serve as permanent regions of growth where cells actively divide
To perform basic metabolism and food storage within the ground tissue

questions.q: Which of the following are classified as complex tissues?
options: Xylem, Phloem, Epidermis, Periderm, and Secretory Cells
Parenchyma, Collenchyma, and Sclerenchyma
Protoderm, Procambium, and Ground Meristem
Cork Cambium, Vascular Cambium, and Apical Meristems

questions.q: What is the structural composition of a vessel element in the xylem at maturity?
options: It is dead and hollow, lacks cytoplasm or organelles, and is surrounded by a thick, lignified secondary cell wall
It is a living cell containing a nucleus and mitochondria to actively pump water
It is a long-lived parenchyma cell used primarily for horizontal food storage
It is a narrow, tapered cell that lacks perforation plates and only transports water through pits

questions.q: How do perforation plates function within xylem vessels?
options: They do not block the flow of fluid between vessel elements, but they may block the movement of objects like fungal spores
They completely seal the ends of the vessel to prevent water from flowing backward
They actively pump dissolved sugars using ATP generated by companion cells
They secrete a lipid-rich waterproofing material called suberin to prevent leakage

questions.q: How do tracheids differ from vessel elements in terms of water movement?
options: Tracheids have closed, tapered ends that overlap, moving water from cell to cell through pits rather than through perforation plates
Tracheids are living at maturity, whereas vessel elements are dead
Tracheids join end-to-end to form continuous open tubes, whereas vessel elements do not
Tracheids are found only in flowering plants, whereas vessel elements are found in all vascular plants

questions.q: What is the function of ray cells in the xylem?
options: They are long-lived parenchyma cells that facilitate lateral transport and function in food storage
They are dead cells that provide vertical support to the plant stem
They are specialized epidermal cells that regulate gas exchange through stomata
They are secretory cells that produce latex and resins to heal wounds

questions.q: What happens to sieve-tube members in the phloem as they reach maturity?
options: They lose their nucleus and many organelles, remaining alive but depending on adjacent companion cells for metabolic support
They die and become hollow, forming rigid tubes reinforced with lignin
They develop thick secondary cell walls to protect the transported sugars from pathogens
They fuse together to form a solid, impermeable barrier against water loss

questions.q: What is the role of companion cells in the phloem?
options: They contain a nucleus and mitochondria, providing metabolic and energy support to help load and unload sugars into the sieve tubes
They act as dead, hollow structural supports for the delicate sieve-tube members
They secrete cutin to waterproof the phloem vascular bundles
They produce the waxy cuticle layer over the plant's epidermis

questions.q: What structures do ferns and cone-bearing trees use in their phloem instead of sieve-tube members and companion cells?
options: They use sieve cells that overlap at their ends, paired with albuminous cells that act equivalently to companion cells
They use rigid vessel elements paired with long-lived parenchyma ray cells
They use completely hollow tracheids supported by thick, lignified secondary walls
They lack phloem entirely and transport sugars through the xylem

questions.q: What is the function of the cutin layer secreted by the epidermis?
options: It is a fatty substance that forms a protective cuticle to prevent water loss and protect against bacteria and disease organisms
It is a sugary substance designed to attract pollinators to the floral nectaries
It is a rigid, lignified layer that provides structural support to the root system
It is an absorptive layer on root hairs that rapidly pulls water from the soil

questions.q: What is the unique characteristic of the epidermis in orchid velamen roots?
options: The epidermis is several cells thick, with the outer cells functioning something like a sponge
The epidermis is completely absent and replaced by a thick layer of woody cork
The epidermis is covered in sharp, lignified trichomes to repel grazing animals
The epidermis is composed entirely of dead guard cells permanently locked open

questions.q: How do guard cells differ from standard epidermal cells?
options: They differ in shape and contain chloroplasts, bordering the stomata to regulate gas exchange
They are dead at maturity and form hollow tubes for water transport
They lack a cell membrane and are completely fused to the waxy cuticle
They are strictly found in the root system where they absorb essential minerals

questions.q: In woody stems and roots, what complex tissue replaces the epidermis as secondary growth ruptures it?
options: The periderm, which is produced by the cork cambium
The primary xylem, which is produced by the apical meristem
The phloem parenchyma, which expands to cover the exposed stem
The glandular trichomes, which form a protective mat over the wood

questions.q: What substance makes cork cells effective at protecting underlying tissues from water loss and temperature extremes?
options: Suberin, a lipid-rich waterproofing material deposited in their cell walls before they die at maturity
Cutin, a waxy secretion produced continuously by living cork cells
Lignin, a rigid structural compound that prevents cork cells from expanding
Mucilage, a sticky glycoprotein that traps moisture around the stem

questions.q: What are lenticels and what is their function in the periderm?
options: Loosely arranged parenchyma cells not impregnated with suberin, functioning in gas exchange between the air and the interior of the stem
Tightly packed cork cells that permanently seal wounds and block fungal spores
Specialized vascular tubes that transport resins and latex to the bark surface
Epidermal hairs that reflect excess light and reduce water loss

questions.q: What are the four primary functions of roots?
options: Anchor the plant, absorb water and minerals, transport compounds between roots and shoots, and store carbohydrates/nutrients
Perform photosynthesis, anchor the plant, produce flowers, and store carbohydrates
Absorb sunlight, release oxygen, transport pollen, and anchor the plant
Regulate gas exchange, perform secondary growth, produce seeds, and absorb water

questions.q: What is the 'Radicle' in plant development?
options: The embryonic root of the plant, contained within the seed embryo
The embryonic stem that develops into the main trunk
The first true leaf to emerge after germination
The protective sheath covering the apical meristem

questions.q: How do adventitious roots differ from a primary taproot?
options: Adventitious roots develop from a stem or leaf rather than from another root
Adventitious roots grow exclusively upwards toward the soil surface
Adventitious roots lack an endodermis and Casparian strip
Adventitious roots form the thick, central woody core of eudicots

questions.q: What are the four distinct regions of a young root (from the tip upwards)?
options: The root cap, the region of cell division, the region of elongation, and the region of maturation
The root cap, the vascular cylinder, the cortex, and the epidermis
The protoderm, the ground meristem, the procambium, and the pith
The apical meristem, the lateral meristem, the intercalary meristem, and the node

questions.q: What are the major functions of the root cap?
options: Protection of the apical meristem, lubrication via mucilage secretion, and gravity perception (gravitropism)
Absorption of water, storage of starch, and initiation of lateral branches
Photosynthesis, gas exchange, and secondary growth
Production of primary xylem, formation of root hairs, and anchoring the plant

questions.q: How does the root cap facilitate movement through the soil?
options: Root cap cells secrete mucilage through dictyosomes (Golgi apparatus) to lubricate the root tip, reducing friction
The root cap hardens into a solid woody point to physically break rocks
The root cap rapidly expands and contracts to push soil particles aside
The root cap absorbs surrounding water, dissolving the soil in front of it

questions.q: How do roots perceive the direction of gravity?
options: Specialized root-cap cells contain amyloplasts that act as gravity sensors by settling at the bottom of the cell
The apical meristem uses light sensors to grow in the opposite direction of the sun
The endodermis shifts its Casparian strips downward to direct water flow
Root hairs physically feel the density of the soil and grow toward higher pressure

questions.q: What occurs in the 'Region of Elongation' in a young root?
options: Cells elongate rapidly, small vacuoles merge to form a large central vacuole (up to 90% of cell volume), and the root is pushed forward through the soil
Cells undergo rapid mitotic division to produce new apical meristem tissue
Cells differentiate into specialized primary tissues like xylem and phloem
Root hairs emerge to begin absorbing water and minerals

questions.q: In which region of the root do root hairs develop?
options: The region of maturation (or differentiation)
The region of elongation
The region of cell division
The root cap

questions.q: What is the primary function of the root cortex?
options: It allows movement of water/nutrients toward the vascular tissue and serves as an important site for carbohydrate storage
It acts as a rigid, lignified protective shell around the root tip
It is the main site of active cell division for root elongation
It generates lateral branch roots directly from its outer layers

questions.q: What is the function of the Casparian strip in the endodermis?
options: It forms a suberin barrier that blocks the apoplastic pathway, forcing water and dissolved solutes to cross a plasma membrane before entering the vascular cylinder
It provides rigid structural support to prevent the root from collapsing under soil pressure
It acts as a nutrient sink, storing excess carbohydrates for winter dormancy
It actively pumps water out of the root to prevent drowning in flooded soils

questions.q: What is the 'Pericycle' and what critical structures arise from it?
options: An important layer of parenchyma tissue directly inside the endodermis; it gives rise to lateral (branch) roots and part of the vascular cambium in dicots
The outermost epidermal layer of the root; it gives rise to root hairs and mucilage
The central core of the monocot root; it stores large amounts of starch and water
A specialized ring of dead cells that protects the xylem from fungal infections

questions.q: How is the primary xylem typically arranged in eudicot and conifer roots?
options: It occupies the center of the root, often forming a star- or X-shaped pattern with arms extending toward the pericycle
It is scattered randomly throughout the entire cortex
It forms a hollow ring surrounding a large central pith
It is located entirely on the outside of the endodermis, forming a protective layer

questions.q: How does the vascular arrangement in monocot roots differ from dicot roots?
options: In monocot roots, the xylem and phloem are arranged in a ring around a central parenchymatous pith
In monocot roots, the xylem forms a solid star shape in the exact center
Monocot roots lack phloem entirely, relying on the cortex for sugar transport
Monocot roots have their vascular bundles scattered randomly throughout the cortex

questions.q: What is the 'Apoplastic' pathway for water movement in roots?
options: Movement through the cell walls and intercellular spaces, offering much less resistance to flow than symplastic movement
Movement directly through the living cytoplasm and plasmodesmata of the cells
Movement strictly through the central vacuole of cortical cells
Movement of water backward from the xylem into the surrounding soil

questions.q: What are the eight main types of specialized root modifications covered in Lecture 8?
options: Food-storage roots, Water-storage roots, Propagative roots, Pneumatophores, Aerial roots, Contractile roots, Buttress roots, and Parasitic roots
Taproots, Fibrous roots, Radicles, Root hairs, Pericycles, Endodermis, Cortex, and Root caps
Tracheids, Vessel elements, Sieve-tube members, Companion cells, Albuminous cells, Sclereids, Fibers, and Ray cells
Chlorenchyma, Aerenchyma, Collenchyma, Sclerenchyma, Protoderm, Procambium, Ground meristem, and Periderm

questions.q: How do 'Food-Storage Roots' function, and how does their anatomical origin differ between carrots/sweet potatoes and beets/turnips/radishes?
options: They enlarge as they accumulate starch, sugars, and other carbohydrates to support future growth, regrowth, flowering, or reproduction; they develop mainly from roots in carrots, cassava, and sweet potatoes, but from both stem and root in many beets, turnips, and radishes
They store purely liquid water for desert survival; carrots and sweet potatoes develop strictly from stem tissue, while beets and turnips develop strictly from root hairs
They shorten to pull the plant deeper into the soil; carrots develop from aerial velamen, while radishes develop from haustoria
They form adventitious buds that grow into genetically identical root suckers in all root vegetables

questions.q: What is the primary function of 'Water-Storage Roots', and what plant is a classic example capable of producing water-storage roots weighing over 25.3 kg?
options: Found in arid or seasonally dry environments, they develop enlarged roots that store water to help the plant survive periods of limited soil moisture; manroot (Marah) is a classic example
Found in waterlogged swamps, they pump excess water out of the plant into the atmosphere; black mangrove (Avicennia germinans) is a classic example
They absorb atmospheric humidity through a multi-layered spongy epidermis; dodder (Cuscuta) is a classic example
They accumulate insoluble starch grains to prevent freezing in arctic tundra soils; cassava is a classic example

questions.q: How do 'Propagative Roots' facilitate reproduction in woody plants such as cherries, apples, pears, and plums?
options: They form adventitious buds on roots growing near the soil surface that develop into new shoots called root suckers; this is vegetative (asexual) reproduction, producing new plants genetically identical to the parent (except for mutations)
They release haploid spores into the soil that fuse with neighboring roots to create genetically diverse hybrid offspring
They penetrate the stems of neighboring fruit trees using haustoria to graft clones onto a host
They contract to pull fallen fruit deeper into the soil so the seeds can germinate safely

questions.q: Why do wetland trees like the black mangrove (Avicennia germinans) require 'Pneumatophores', and how do these specialized roots work?
options: Waterlogged soils have little available oxygen (because gases diffuse much more slowly through water than air), limiting aerobic respiration; pneumatophores ('breathing roots') grow upward from underground roots above the waterlogged soil, using lenticels and internal air spaces to move atmospheric oxygen to submerged tissues
Waterlogged soils lack nitrogen; pneumatophores grow downward into the bedrock to house nitrogen-fixing rhizobia bacteria
Pneumatophores are large, vertically flattened roots that distribute mechanical forces across shallow tropical soils to prevent tipping
Pneumatophores are aerial clinging roots that attach mangrove seedlings to floating logs

questions.q: Match the four distinct types of 'Aerial Roots'—Orchid aerial roots, Prop/brace roots, Clinging roots, and Photosynthetic roots—with their specific functions and examples:
options: Orchid aerial roots: have a velamen that absorbs water/nutrients and protects against drying; Prop/brace roots: support plants like corn and banyan trees; Clinging roots: attach climbing plants like ivy to surfaces; Photosynthetic roots: produce sugars in some orchids and epiphytes
Orchid aerial roots: pull bulbs deeper into soil; Prop/brace roots: penetrate host xylem; Clinging roots: breathe in waterlogged mangrove swamps; Photosynthetic roots: store 25 kg of water
All four types of aerial roots function exclusively to anchor large tropical trees against wind throw
Prop roots attach ivy to walls, whereas clinging roots support tall corn stalks

questions.q: How do 'Contractile Roots' work, which plants commonly have them, and what four environmental hazards do they protect underground organs from?
options: Common in plants with bulbs or corms (lilies, onions, gladioli, crocuses), they shorten to pull the underground organ deeper into the soil to a stable depth, protecting it from temperature extremes, drought, frost, and soil-surface disturbance
Common in tropical trees, they expand outward to push the trunk higher above floodwaters, protecting against waterlogging, pathogens, insects, and wind
Common in legumes, they coil into a 'shepherd's crook' to trap soil bacteria and protect against nitrogen deficiency
Common in epiphytic orchids, they contract to squeeze rainwater out of the velamen into the vascular cylinder

questions.q: What are 'Buttress Roots', where are they commonly found, and what are their primary functions?
options: Large, vertically flattened roots extending from the lower trunk across the soil surface; common in large tropical trees with shallow, spreading root systems, they increase stability by distributing mechanical forces over a wider area (preventing tipping) and may increase surface area for water and nutrient uptake
Deep taproots that penetrate over 50 meters into desert aquifers to store water for dry seasons
Spongy upward-growing roots covered in lenticels that supply oxygen to submerged mangrove roots
Adventitious roots that sprout genetically identical suckers from the base of cherry and plum trees

questions.q: How do 'Parasitic Roots' (such as those on scaldweed/dodder, Cuscuta gronovii) obtain resources from host plants?
options: Parasitic plants (some nonphotosynthetic, others photosynthetic) use specialized structures called haustoria—which Cuscuta produces from its stem where it contacts the host—to penetrate host tissues and connect with the host's xylem, phloem, or both
They form a mutualistic fungal mantle around the host root, trading phosphorus for host sugars
They secrete flavonoids to induce the host plant to grow nitrogen-fixing root nodules
They wrap around the host's подземный bulb and contract, pulling the host deeper into the soil until it dies

questions.q: What does the word 'Mycorrhiza' literally mean, what type of ecological relationship is it, and how widespread is it among plants?
options: It means 'fungus-root' (or 'fungal root'); it is a symbiotic (mutualistic) relationship between fungi and plant roots present in more than 95% of plants
It means 'breathing-root'; it is a parasitic relationship affecting less than 5% of wetland plants
It means 'bacterial-nodule'; it is a commensal relationship restricted exclusively to the legume family
It means 'sugar-root'; it is an asexual reproductive structure found in fruit trees

questions.q: In the Plant-Mycorrhizae symbiosis, what specific benefits does the plant receive, and what does the fungus receive in return?
options: The fungus absorbs and concentrates phosphorus (P) much better than root hairs and often forms a mantle of millions of threadlike strands (hyphae) that facilitate water and nutrient absorption; the plant furnishes sugars and amino acids without which the fungus cannot survive
The fungus fixes atmospheric nitrogen ($N_2$) into ammonia using nitrogenase; the plant provides phosphorus and water to the fungus
The fungus performs photosynthesis to supply the plant with carbohydrates; the plant provides a protective suberin coat
The fungus penetrates neighbouring plants with haustoria; the plant provides ATP and flavonoids

questions.q: How do 'Ectomycorrhizae' (ectotrophic) and 'Endomycorrhizae' (endotrophic) differ in structure and host plant distribution?
options: In Ectomycorrhizae (common in trees like pines and oaks), fungal hyphae penetrate the root cortex between cells without entering the cells and form a thin encrusting 'mantle' on the root surface; in Endomycorrhizae (found in the majority of woody and herbaceous land plants), hyphae invade the cortex cells and no mantle is present
In Ectomycorrhizae, hyphae invade the interior of cortex cells and lack a mantle; in Endomycorrhizae, hyphae remain strictly outside the cells and form a thick surface mantle
Ectomycorrhizae are found in 95% of herbaceous crops like corn and basil, whereas Endomycorrhizae are restricted to pines and oaks
Ectomycorrhizae fix nitrogen in root nodules, whereas Endomycorrhizae absorb oxygen in waterlogged soils

questions.q: What is the composition of Earth's atmosphere by gas percentage, and why can't plants easily use atmospheric nitrogen directly without fixation?
options: The air is 78% Nitrogen ($N_2$), 21% Oxygen ($O_2$), 0.96% Other Gases (mostly Argon), and 0.04% Carbon Dioxide ($CO_2$); atmospheric $N_2$ consists of two nitrogen atoms bound by a strong triple bond that must be converted (fixed) into ammonia ($NH_3$) or nitrogen compounds
The air is 78% Oxygen, 21% Carbon Dioxide, and 0.04% Nitrogen; nitrogen is too scarce in the air for plants to absorb
The air is 50% Nitrogen and 50% Methane ($CH_4$); plants absorb $N_2$ gas directly through their stomata without bacteria
The air is 78% Ammonia ($NH_3$), which is toxic to roots unless converted into $N_2$ gas

questions.q: How does industrial nitrogen fixation via the 'Haber-Bosch Process' work, and what is its major environmental drawback?
options: It is an oxidation-reduction reaction that heats $N_2$ gas to $500^\circ\text{C}$ at high pressure (500 PSI / 300 bar) with hydrogen derived from natural gas (methane, $CH_4$) to yield ammonia ($NH_3$), requiring large amounts of non-renewable energy
It uses genetically modified rhizobia bacteria in unheated open-air ponds to convert water into nitrate with zero energy input
It freezes liquid air to extract argon and carbon dioxide at room temperature using solar power
It burns coal to convert soil phosphorus into gaseous nitrogen at $100^\circ\text{C}$

questions.q: What is the nature of the symbiotic association between Rhizobia bacteria and Legume plants?
options: It is mutually beneficial: the legume plant provides energy (sugars, carbohydrates, and ATP from photosynthesis) for the rhizobia to fix atmospheric $N_2$, and the rhizobia provide fixed nitrogen compounds to the host plant for protein production
The rhizobia bacteria provide sugars and ATP to the legume, while the legume provides atmospheric $N_2$ to the bacteria
It is a parasitic infection where rhizobia destroy the root cortex using haustoria without benefiting the legume
The bacteria form an ectotrophic mantle to absorb phosphorus, while the legume supplies suberin

questions.q: During Step 1 and Step 2 of establishing the legume-rhizobia symbiosis (Root Signals and NodD Activation), what compounds do legume roots excrete and how do rhizobia sense them?
options: Legume roots and germinating seeds excrete attractant compounds including vitamins, sugars, amino acids, choline, and flavonoids; the stimulated bacterial nod (nodulation) gene produces the NodD protein, which acts as the sensor that recognizes the plant's flavonoids and activates bacterial nod genes
Legume roots excrete nitrogenase enzymes; the bacteria use nif genes on their flagella to swim away from the flavonoids
Rhizobia excrete flavonoids into the soil, which bind to the plant's Rubisco protein to trigger seed germination
Legume roots secrete mucilage from the root cap to dissolve the bacterial cell wall

questions.q: During Step 3 and Step 4 of nodulation (Nod Factors, Infection, and Nodulation), how are molecular cues regulated and what physical changes occur in the root hair?
options: Molecular cues are positively autoregulated (flavonoids stimulate bacterial Nod factor production, which in turn stimulates more plant flavonoid secretion); bacterial Nod factors induce root hair deformation into a pronounced curl called a 'shepherd's crook', initiating an infection thread that leads to a developing root nodule
Molecular cues are negatively feedback-inhibited; Nod factors cause the root hairs to straighten and slough off, blocking bacterial entry
Nod factors dissolve the Casparian strip, allowing bacteria to enter the xylem vessels directly without curling the root hair
The plant's cortex cells form a fungal mantle around the bacteria to prevent an infection thread from forming

questions.q: What determines host-plant specificity in rhizobia bacteria, and what is the exact biochemical equation catalyzed by the 'nitrogenase' enzyme (encoded by nif genes) inside the root nodule?
options: Specificity is determined by the number of Nod genes in the bacteria (one Nod gene = highly specific; multiple Nod genes = can inoculate multiple plant species); nitrogenase catalyzes: $N_2 + 8H^+ + 8e^- + 16\text{ ATP} \rightarrow 2\text{ NH}_3 + H_2 + 16\text{ ADP} + 16\text{ P}_i$
Specificity is determined by root depth; nitrogenase catalyzes: $CH_4 + H_2O \rightarrow CO + 3H_2$ at $500^\circ\text{C}$ without requiring ATP
Specificity is determined by the size of the root cap; nitrogenase consumes 2 ATP to convert $NH_3$ into $N_2$ gas
All rhizobia have identical specificity and use 100 ATP molecules per molecule of $O_2$ produced

questions.q: What is 'Indeterminate Growth' in plants, and how do apical and lateral meristems contribute to it?
options: The ability of plants to continue producing new organs throughout their lives because some meristems remain active; apical meristems at shoot/root tips produce primary growth (increasing length) while lateral meristems produce secondary growth (increasing thickness)
Growth that permanently stops once the plant reaches a fixed adult size; apical meristems increase stem thickness while lateral meristems increase stem length
Growth that continues at a constant rate even during unfavorable winter conditions without ever pausing
The production of adventitious roots exclusively from mature dead sclerenchyma fibers

questions.q: On a plant stem, what are 'Nodes', 'Internodes', 'Axils', and 'Axillary Buds'?
options: Nodes are the regions on the stem where leaves attach; Internodes are the stem sections between nodes; an Axil is the angle between a petiole and the stem; an Axillary Bud is the bud located in the axil that can develop into branches or next season's flowers
Nodes are the stem sections between leaves; Internodes are the exact points where petioles attach; Axillary buds are located at the tip of the root cap
Nodes are specialized structures inside the xylem; Internodes are gaps in the vascular cambium; Axils are paired leaflike appendages
Nodes only occur on roots, while Internodes and Axillary Buds only occur on monocot leaves

questions.q: How do Stems and Roots compare in terms of vascular tissues, nodes/internodes, and cuticles?
options: Both contain xylem and phloem connecting shoot and root systems; stems have nodes, internodes, and typically a waxy cuticle on exposed surfaces, whereas roots lack nodes and internodes and their young absorbing regions generally lack a cuticle to allow water uptake
Stems contain only phloem and lack a cuticle, whereas roots contain only xylem and have a thick waxy cuticle on their root hairs
Both stems and roots have nodes, internodes, and axillary buds, but only roots possess a waxy cuticle
Stems lack xylem and phloem entirely, relying on the epidermis for all vertical water transport

questions.q: On the external form of a woody twig, what are the 'Blade', 'Petiole', and 'Stipules'?
options: The blade is the flattened part of the leaf; the petiole is the stalk that attaches the leaf to the twig; stipules are paired, often somewhat leaflike appendages at the base of a leaf that may remain throughout the leaf's life or fall off in spring leaving tiny stipule scars
The blade is the stalk attaching the leaf to the stem; the petiole is the flattened photosynthetic surface; stipules are pores in the periderm used for gas exchange
Stipules are protective scales covering the terminal bud; the petiole is the scar left behind when a branch breaks off
All three are internal vascular tissues produced by the procambium inside the stem pith

questions.q: What is the function of a 'Terminal Bud' and 'Bud Scales' on a woody twig, and what marks do bud scales leave behind?
options: Meristems within terminal buds at the twig tip normally produce tissues that make the twig grow longer during the growing season; bud scales protect the buds and fall off when bud tissue starts to grow in the spring, leaving rings of tiny bud scale scars around the twig
Terminal buds are located in the leaf axils and only produce flowers; bud scales remain permanently attached to the twig for the life of the tree
Terminal buds increase the radial girth of the bark; bud scales turn into green photosynthetic leaves in the summer
Bud scales are vascular strands inside the leaf scar, also known as bundle scars

questions.q: On a deciduous woody twig, what are 'Leaf Scars' and 'Bundle Scars'?
options: A leaf scar is the mark left on the stem at a node after a leaf falls off, and bundle scars are tiny marks within the leaf scar showing where vascular traces (strands of xylem and phloem) passed from the stem into the leaf petiole
Leaf scars are openings in the bark for gas exchange (lenticels), and bundle scars are rings left by terminal bud scales
Leaf scars are parenchyma-filled gaps inside the central pith, and bundle scars are axillary buds
Bundle scars are marks left by falling stipules, and leaf scars are caused by insect herbivory

questions.q: How does the shoot apical meristem behave before the growing season begins, and how is it protected?
options: The apical meristem at the stem tip (and in the embryonic stem of a seed prior to germination) is dormant before the growing season begins; it is protected by the bud scales of the bud in which it is located and, to a certain extent, by leaf primordia
The shoot apical meristem divides rapidly all winter long and is protected by a thimble-shaped root cap secreting mucilage
The shoot apical meristem dies at the end of each autumn and is regenerated from cork cambium in the spring
It is protected exclusively by a thick layer of suberized bark and sclereid stone cells

questions.q: What three primary meristems are produced by the shoot apical meristem, and what five 'primary tissues' do they give rise to?
options: 1) Protoderm -> Epidermis; 2) Ground meristem -> Primary ground tissues (Pith and Cortex); 3) Procambium -> Primary xylem and Primary phloem (making five primary tissues: epidermis, pith, cortex, primary xylem, and primary phloem)
1) Protoderm -> Periderm and Cork; 2) Ground meristem -> Secondary xylem and Secondary phloem; 3) Procambium -> Pith
1) Vascular cambium -> Wood; 2) Cork cambium -> Bark; 3) Intercalary meristem -> Leaf primordia
The shoot apical meristem produces only bud primordia and does not produce protoderm, ground meristem, or procambium

questions.q: In a developing shoot tip, where do 'Leaf Primordia' and 'Bud Primordia' originate, and what are 'Leaf Gaps' and 'Bud Gaps'?
options: The shoot apical meristem initiates leaf primordia, and bud primordia form in the leaf axils (developing into axillary buds); as each new leaf or bud receives a vascular trace (strand of xylem and phloem) branching from the stem's vascular cylinder, it leaves a leaf gap or bud gap in the cylinder filled with parenchyma tissue
Leaf gaps and bud gaps are hollow air cavities in the epidermis caused by insects eating the leaf primordia
Leaf primordia develop from the pericycle deep inside the stem, and leaf gaps are filled with dead lignified fibers
Bud primordia form at the base of the root system, and bud gaps are perforation plates inside xylem vessels

questions.q: How does the 'Vascular Cambium' form in a stem, and what tissues does it produce toward the center versus toward the outside?
options: A narrow band of cells between the primary xylem and primary phloem retains its meristematic nature to become the vascular cambium, dividing indefinitely to add girth: it produces secondary xylem (water-conducting cells, fibers, parenchyma) toward the center and secondary phloem (sugar-conducting cells, associated living cells, parenchyma) toward the outside

Marginal Cost is minimized while Marginal Benefit is maximized

An incentive to eliminate labor specialization and encourage autarky

Through central administrative committees issuing physical production quotas

Through international treaties that dictate supply targets for basic resources

Industry trade associations setting mandatory producer prices

Market prices are too volatile to communicate meaningful economic information

Soviet economies relied on competitive auctions for all raw materials

Unprofitable firms receive public subsidies to preserve market diversity
Firms consciously mutate their business structures regardless of market pricing

Private firms are legally prohibited from adopting environmentally conscious practices
Competitive markets guarantee subsidies to unprofitable companies

Rely on voluntary self-restraint while keeping existing market incentives identical
Instruct businesses to disregard production costs and maximize gross output

Free markets would perpetually lower the relative price of staple agricultural crops
Resource exhaustion was impossible due to infinite capital substitution

Global consumption rates of energy and industrial materials systematically declined after 1800

questions.q: What defines an economic 'externality'?
options: An activity that creates a cost or benefit for others that is not reflected in the decision-maker's incentives
The difference between total revenue and marginal cost in a competitive market
A government tax imposed on imported goods and services
A situation where consumer demand perfectly equals producer supply

questions.q: How do negative externalities affect market production levels?
options: The Marginal Social Cost is greater than the Marginal Private Cost (MSC > MPC), leading the market to produce too much of the activity
The Marginal Social Cost is less than the Marginal Private Cost (MSC < MPC), leading the market to produce too little of the activity
The market completely halts production until the external costs are removed
Production levels remain perfectly efficient but prices drop significantly

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a negative externality in forest management?

Delaying harvest to increase carbon storage for climate mitigation
Sharing forest inventory data with other users
Conducting fuel treatments that reduce wildfire risk to neighboring properties

questions.q: How does a Pigouvian tax internalize a negative externality?

It forces consumers to pay a premium directly to the affected third parties
It legally limits the production quantity to zero to eliminate the cost entirely

The Marginal Social Benefit equals the Marginal Private Benefit (MSB = MPB), leading to efficient production
The market produces an overabundance of the activity because it generates free benefits

Converting all public goods into common-pool resources
